<header class="dg-head dg-head-section"><p class="dg-kicker">Appendix B <span class="dg-sep">•</span> <a href="index.html">Proofs &amp; Comments</a></p><h1 class="dg-title"><span class="dg-secnum">B.9</span> Connections and covariant derivatives (§<a class="dg-xref" href="../covariant-derivative/connections-affine-manifolds.html" data-kind="section" data-label="section_Connections_Affine_Manifolds">6.1</a>)</h1></header>
<p>In Chapter <a class="dg-xref" href="../covariant-derivative/index.html" data-kind="chapter" data-label="chapter_Covariant_Derivative">6</a> the words <em>connection</em> and <em>covariant derivative</em> are used almost interchangeably: the connection is the structure <span class="math inline">\(\nabla\)</span>, and the covariant derivative is what it produces, <span class="math inline">\(\nabla_\mathcal{X} T\)</span>. In differential geometry at large, however, the two notions are genuinely different, the connection being the more general one. This appendix sketches the difference.</p>
<ul class="dg-itemize dg-depth-1">
<li><p><strong>Connections live on any bundle.</strong> Consider a smooth bundle <span class="math inline">\(E \xrightarrow{\pi} \mathcal{M}\)</span>, with arbitrary fibres. At each point <span class="math inline">\(e\)</span> of the total space, the tangent space <span class="math inline">\(T_eE\)</span> contains a canonical <em>vertical</em> subspace, <span class="math inline">\(V_eE \coloneqq \ker (d\pi)_e\)</span>, made of the directions along the fibre, which the projection collapses to zero. There is, however, no canonical notion of <em>horizontal</em> direction, i.e. of moving along <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{M}\)</span> without moving within the fibre. A (Ehresmann) <strong>connection</strong> is precisely such a choice: a smooth assignment of horizontal subspaces <span class="math inline">\(H_eE\)</span> complementary to the vertical ones,  <span class="math display">\[
            T_eE = V_eE \oplus H_eE .
        \]</span>  From it one obtains <em>parallel transport</em>: a curve in <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{M}\)</span> can be lifted uniquely to a horizontal curve in <span class="math inline">\(E\)</span> through any chosen point of the initial fibre. Nothing in this construction requires the fibres to be vector spaces. On a principal <span class="math inline">\(G\)</span>-bundle one additionally demands compatibility with the action of <span class="math inline">\(G\)</span>, and the connection can be equivalently encoded as a Lie-algebra-valued 1-form.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>Covariant derivatives live on vector bundles.</strong> A covariant derivative is a linear differential operator acting on sections of a vector bundle <span class="math inline">\(E \xrightarrow{\pi} \mathcal{M}\)</span>,  <span class="math display">\[
            \nabla : \Gamma T\mathcal{M} \times \Gamma E \longrightarrow \Gamma E,
        \]</span>  <span class="math inline">\(C^\infty(\mathcal{M})\)</span>-linear in its first argument and satisfying the product rule <span class="math inline">\(\nabla_\mathcal{X}(g\,s) = \mathcal{X}\left\lfloor g \right\rceil s + g \, \nabla_\mathcal{X} s\)</span> in its second one. Both properties require adding sections and multiplying them by scalar fields, which only makes sense when the fibres are vector spaces.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>Where they meet.</strong> On a vector bundle, the connections whose horizontal subspaces are compatible with the linear structure of the fibres (<em>linear</em> connections) are in one-to-one correspondence with covariant derivatives: <span class="math inline">\(\nabla_\mathcal{X} s\)</span> is the vertical part of the derivative of the section <span class="math inline">\(s\)</span> along <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{X}\)</span>, the vertical subspaces of a vector bundle being canonically identified with the fibres themselves. A connection is therefore more general in two ways: it exists on bundles where covariant derivatives cannot even be defined, most notably principal bundles, and even on vector bundles there are non-linear connections that yield no covariant derivative.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>A physics example.</strong> In gauge theories the gauge potential <span class="math inline">\(A\)</span> is a connection on a principal <span class="math inline">\(G\)</span>-bundle, not a derivative of anything. The familiar covariant derivative <span class="math inline">\(D_j = \partial_j - i A_j\)</span> only appears when <span class="math inline">\(A\)</span> acts on matter fields, which are sections of associated vector bundles.</p></li>
</ul>
<p>In general relativity all the relevant objects are sections of the tangent bundle and of the tensor bundles built from it, which are vector bundles. There the two notions coincide, and the connection can be defined directly through the axioms of a covariant derivative, as done in Chapter <a class="dg-xref" href="../covariant-derivative/index.html" data-kind="chapter" data-label="chapter_Covariant_Derivative">6</a>.</p>
